question: The Commission’s answer to question E-002879/20231 does not answer the question as to whether an amendment to the Habitats Directive to allow the hunting of wolves would entail a simultaneous update of Annexes II and IV to the Habitats Directive so that all species that are currently red-listed would be added to the annexes. 1.

Will the Commission state whether it is aware of whether the Member States’ legal implementation of the obligation under Directive 98/58/EC of 20 July 1998 concerning the protection of animals kept for farming purposes to protect livestock against predatory attacks – among other things – has been adequately implemented in the respective Member States, and whether it has an overview of the practical implementation of that obligation in the relevant Member States?

Will the Commission submit an information note describing the Member States’ practical implementation or, alternatively, state whether it takes the view that relaxing the protection of wolves – without at the same ensuring that the obligation to fence livestock in, for example, is met – is a professionally serious approach to resolving the serious conflict between a growing wolf population and the protection of livestock against attacks?

Will the Commission answer the question set out in E-002879/2023 as to whether the Annex to the Habitats Directive will be amended to allow the hunting of wolves as part of a general update of the annexes to the directive on the basis of a strictly professional approach?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.3.2024) 1. Member States are primarily responsible for the implementation of Directive 98/58/EC concerning the protection of animals kept for farming purposes1. The Commission performs regular audits and controls on the correct implementation and enforcement of the provisions in EU animal welfare legislation.

The results of these controls and audits have not identified any issue on the implementation of the requirement related to the protection of farmed animals against predators. 2. Based on the above, the Commission sees no immediate need to issue an information note on the protection of farmed animals against predators.

A change in the legal protection of the wolf would not remove the need and the importance to invest in prevention measures to reduce livestock predation risks. It is for the competent national authorities to implement the most appropriate measures in view of the specific circumstances. 3. At present, there are no plans to conduct a review of the Habitats Directive's2 Annexes.

The proposal of 20 December 2023 to change the protection status of the wolf under the Bern Convention3 was made on the basis of a dedicated in-depth analysis targeting a species that has been showing a fast recovery in the EU and is associated with most human-wildlife conflicts.
1 Council Directive 98/58/EC of 20 July 1998 concerning the protection of animals kept for farming purposes,

OJ L 221, 8.8.1998, p. 23–27. 2 Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, p. 7–50. 3 https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_23_6752
